One game that comes to my mind is Mushroom 11. The game has its share of problems (some more difficult stunts can't be executed very consistently and a few parts are tedious) but one thing it does right is show how many applications a simple eraser tool and its smaller variation (and that's what the controls are limited to) have and how they combine with growing back mechanic. Uses of this tool range from tasks as simple as moving around and climbing stuff to tasks as complex as making bridges for objects to roll over or shaping the blob in a shape of a handle.

Anyone else knows some very throughout game concept or stage gimmick exploration?
Are there any games where you're surprised how thoroughly the game explores its central concepts and/or gimmicks inside levels?

Hmm, I'm not sure it's considered a gimmick, but I remember being impressed at how consistently Half-Life 2 implemented puzzles throughout the story. At the time I was expecting a typical first-person story game with the emphasis on shooting, but the puzzles served as a great way to unwind between action segments and keep the game interesting.

The only problem for me is that I kept forgetting it was a puzzle game. "Why the hell can't I get into the next area? Is this game broken? OH, I keep forgetting this is a puzzle game. I bet I have to use those 55-gallon drums somehow"

There was a game called Bulletstorm where you had this kind of laser lasso you could use to snatch up enemies and pull them towards the player while you shot at them, lasso and then boot the enemy into a cactus or electric fence or meat grinder, there were just 100 ways the devs figured out on how to use that laser lasso.

Honestly, I'm pretty much tired of FPS games but I had so much fun with BulletStorm. I wonder if it's on Steam...

I was consistently impressed with how Braid explored it's design space. Every single puzzle required you to learn a new skill. There wasn't any extra fluff. The Witness a bit less so.
VVVVVV and Catherine for me. They took the simple concepts of gravity flipping/block pushing and made entire games out of them. And it worked!

I know the autistic fanbase has made many gamers quite wary of Undertale, but for what effectively looks like a glorified RPG Maker game in many regards, the sheer amount of detail and the many, many hidden secrets in it are quite baffling.

I also was quite fond of how TloZ: Ocarina of Time actually made the tim-travelling aspect important for many side-quests and smaller secrets.
Planescape: Torment. An absolute piece of art. A god among gods.

Fallout 3, I may just be nostalgic as this was my introduction to the world of fallout. It really resonated with me being lurched into chaos, where you and your character are completely clueless about whats happening. Exploring the Capital Wasteland was always great fun and nerve wracking when starting out, I spent many hours skulking up hills for a proper vantage point all the while anticipating the next predator sneak attack and only having a 10mm pistol and .32 rifle as defense. But the random easter eggs, settlements, and NPCs add so much depth to the overall desperation and fucky-ness of surviving in a post-apocalyptic meat grinder. I also really like the depressing scenes you discover at random, like the suicides and random child sized skeletons in their bedrooms. It evokes a very somber reminder of just how many people suffered horrendous fates in that story.
Red Faction Guerilla took destructible buildings to a whole new level that hasn't been reached since. That was pretty much the one thing that kept an otherwise bland third person shooter fun.

I'm almost certain that this battery will change its battery layout / circuitry based on the load that's applied, as the voltage can change based on series or parallel hookups. It says it can support USB devices, 12V devices, and even 120V AC devices as well. To do this, the battery would then have to change it's battery layout internally as the need arises.
